neighbours.label: the future or conditional auxiliary chain 'will/would (have)' in a plan or counterfactual, peaking on 'have'/'had' where an obligation ('have to', 'require') is the expected continuation, as against present-tense statements of the same need
fire: To finish on time, the builders will have to work through the weekend.
To win the league, the team would have had to beat both rivals in April.
If prices keep rising, many families will have to cut back on heating.
To meet the target, the city would have to double its bus fleet.
To stay open, the library will have to find a new source of funding.
Without the loan, the farm would have had to sell half its cattle.
To pass the bill, the government will have to win over the senators.
To reach the summit by noon, the climbers would have to leave at four.
quiet: The builders are working through the weekend because the deadline is close.
The team beat both rivals in April and won the league.
Rising prices mean many families are cutting back on heating.
The city doubled its bus fleet last year to meet the target.
The library found a new source of funding and stayed open.
Thanks to the loan, the farm kept all of its cattle.
The government won over the senators and passed the bill.
The climbers left at four and reached the summit by noon.

predictions: fire 0.4-0.7 on 'have'/'had' in 'will have to' / 'would have had to'; present-tense 'needs to' and plain past sentences below 0.15
notes: Card peaks: ' had' in 'we would have had to start', ' have' in 'Detroit will have to begin', ' requires', ' would' x9 before 'require'/'take'; the - pole promotes ' required', ' need'. Probe: 'will have to repopulate' 0.700, 'would have had to start' 0.667, 'would have liked to' 0.639 (so not obligation-specific), 'will try to' 0.422, 'would require' 0.381; 'would offer a pleasant path' 0.071, 'You need a motor' 0.053.
